children.text: Dr. Brad’s Full Story Synergy Spine and Nerve Center

Dr. Brad Fackrell shares the full story of how chiropractic transformed his health from severe asthma and daily medication to a drug-free life, and why he became a chiropractor.
From wrestling injuries to severe asthma to drug-free, the full story of how chiropractic changed Dr. Brad's life.

When I was 16 years old I went to see a chiropractor because I had hurt my back in a wrestling accident. This chiropractor was great. He helped me get out of pain and get back on the wrestling mat. (It didn't make me a better wrestler though.) I remember getting adjusted by him for at least a month or so 3 times a week.

The problem was that the care I received was not specific and it didn't begin with the right purpose. His purpose was to get me out of pain and therefore, that was my purpose too. It worked wonderfully too… for getting me out of pain.

But then about 8 years later I was introduced to a different chiropractor that took x-rays so that I could see how subluxation was interfering with my life. More importantly, he was able to see how to adjust me specifically so that it would really change my life.

I am so grateful for the education that this chiropractor gave me. He helped me to take control of my life. He literally saved my life. Chiropractic became a part of my life at the age of 24 and I have never looked back.

About 8 months after starting wellness specific chiropractic care I was taking about half of the medication that I had to take before. This had never happened to me before. I was able to continue to decrease the medication and now in my mid forties I don't have a medical doctor that gives me prescriptions. Unless something environmental triggers it, I am drug-free.
This is why I became a chiropractor and why I practice the way that I do. Chiropractic is so much more than just sore necks and backs.
The full personal story of Dr. Brad Fackrell, from a teenage wrestling injury to severe asthma to a drug-free life through wellness chiropractic care.

children.text: Auto Accident & Whiplash Chiropractor in Albuquerque, NM

Albuquerque is New Mexico's largest city and the heart of the metro Synergy Spine and Nerve Center serves every day. If you are searching for auto-accident and whiplash care near Albuquerque, NM (87102), Synergy Spine and Nerve Center is about 20 minutes from Albuquerque. We serve Northeast Heights, Nob Hill, North Valley from 1453 Rio Rancho Blvd, Suite 2 — not a pop-up franchise. Nearby searches we also rank pages for include “chiropractor albuquerque,” “chiropractor albuquerque westside,” and “family chiropractor albuquerque.” Patients comparing Absolute, Lundgren, CareMore, Lifetime, or The Joint still need a clinic that exams before it sells a plan. That is this office.
How this care works
A prompt post-accident exam.
Imaging when warranted (or referral if findings suggest it).
Documentation that satisfies attorneys and insurers, we know the paperwork.
A graded care plan from acute to recovery to function.

Whiplash is a soft-tissue and joint injury caused by a rapid back-and-forth motion of the head, most commonly in a rear-end collision. The classic mistake is to skip evaluation because 'nothing feels broken.' Whiplash symptoms often appear 24–72 hours later, and untreated whiplash is the single biggest predictor of chronic neck pain a decade later.
Getting here from Albuquerque
From Albuquerque the drive is about 20 minutes via the Westside / Coors / Paseo corridors to Rio Rancho. Parking is on-site; you are not circling a downtown garage.

From Albuquerque, set navigation to 1453 Rio Rancho Blvd, Suite 2, Rio Rancho, NM 87124. Nearby reference points: Old Town, Sandia Peak Tramway, ABQ BioPark. Office hours are Monday 8:00–5:30, Tuesday 1:00–5:00, Wednesday 10:00–5:30, Thursday 1:00–5:30. Closed Friday–Sunday. Call (505) 891-2280 if you need the first appointment after a long drive.
Why patients come in
Albuquerque patients often sit I-40 or the river crossing twice a day. That commute is a classic driver of disc, sciatica, and tech-neck cases we see every week.

After a crash on I-25, US-550, Coors, or Rio Rancho Blvd, Albuquerque drivers should be documented within 72 hours. Whiplash often blooms on day two. We exam, image when needed, and write notes insurers actually use.
Any {city}-area driver or passenger involved in a recent collision, even low-speed. Don't wait for symptoms to set in before getting documented.
What to expect
Documentation suitable for insurance or legal counsel
Care coordinated with your attorney if you have one
A clear timeline and goal, re-evaluated every 12 visits
When to seek care
Pain from Albuquerque that lasts more than a few days, interrupts sleep, or shoots into an arm or leg
A recent auto accident on local roads or I-25 / US-550 even if you “feel fine” today

meta.title: Car Accident Recovery Guide for Rio Rancho Drivers

records.heroHeading: Car Accident Recovery Guide for Rio Rancho Drivers
records.excerpt: Track key symptoms after a crash, learn when imaging is needed, and when to visit a car accident chiropractor in Rio Rancho for care and relief.

children.text: The first few days after a car accident can be confusing. You might step out of the car, feel a little shaken, and think you are fine, then wake up the next morning with a stiff neck, tight shoulders, or a pounding headache that was not there before.

Those early hours matter more than most people realize. Pain and stiffness often show up late, and small issues can grow if they are ignored. In this guide, we will walk through what to watch for in the first 72 hours, when imaging might be helpful, and when a car accident chiropractor in Rio Rancho may be a smart next step.

Here in Rio Rancho, late summer often means heavier traffic, back-to-school runs, and weekend trips on busy roads. More cars can mean more fender benders. Knowing what to look for in your own body after a crash can help you protect your long-term health.
Hidden Symptoms in the First 24 Hours

Right after a collision, your body is full of adrenaline. That stress response can hide pain. Soft tissues, like muscles and ligaments, can be stretched or irritated, but you might not feel much until hours later, once things start to swell.
Some common injuries that can stay quiet at first include:
Whiplash injuries to the neck
Muscle strains in the neck, shoulders, or back
Ligament sprains around the spine or shoulders
Mild concussions or head injuries

Even if your pain feels minor, pay close attention if you notice neck stiffness or trouble turning your head, headaches (especially starting at the base of the skull), dizziness, nausea, or feeling "foggy." Other signals include jaw pain or clicking when you chew, visual changes such as blurriness or light sensitivity, tightness across the shoulders or upper back, and tingling or numbness in your arms, hands, or fingers.

A simple 24-hour self check can help you track changes. Rate your pain from 0 to 10 and note where it is, pay attention to headache patterns and dizziness, notice how well you sleep that first night, and see if you can turn your head and lift your arms like normal.
There are also red flags that are not okay to wait on. You should seek urgent or emergency care right away if you notice:
Loss of consciousness, even briefly
Worsening confusion or trouble speaking
Severe or rapidly increasing headache
Repeated vomiting
Chest pain or trouble breathing
Loss of bowel or bladder control
Growing weakness in your arms or legs
These can be signs of more serious injury and need prompt medical attention.
The 24- to 72-Hour Window: Pain, Swelling, and Stiffness
As you move into days two and three after the crash, inflammation and muscle guarding often increase. That is why many people say they feel worse on day two than they did right after the collision.
Typical patterns we see after a car accident include:
Morning stiffness in the neck and upper back
Mid-back or low-back aching after sitting for a while
Fatigue by late afternoon
Headaches that build through the day

Light, smart movement usually helps more than total bed rest. To support healing in this window, change positions often so you do not sit or stand in one spot for long. You can also use ice on sore areas for short periods (with a cloth between your skin and the cold), pay attention to posture when you work or drive (keep your head over your shoulders, not poked forward), and use both hands when lifting light objects while keeping them close to your body.

Some choices can slow healing or aggravate your injury, such as pushing through pain at the gym or going straight back to heavy lifting, taking long road trips without breaks to stretch, or overusing pain medications to hide symptoms instead of respecting your limits. Pain is your body's way of asking for a change, and listening early can help the healing process go more smoothly.
When You Really Need Imaging After a Crash

Many people wonder if they should get X-rays or an MRI after a car accident. Different types of imaging look at different things, and not everyone needs every kind. Here is a simple way to think of it:
X-ray: Shows bones. Often used to look for fractures or major joint problems.
MRI: Shows soft tissues, like discs, muscles, ligaments, and nerves.
CT scan: Gives detailed images of bones and some soft tissues, usually ordered for more serious injuries.
Imaging should be strongly considered if:
There is concern for a fracture from the force of the crash
You have severe or progressive numbness, tingling, or weakness
You notice loss of coordination or changes in walking
You have strong, focused pain right on the spine that is not easing
Pain is not improving at all after several days or is getting worse

Many soft-tissue injuries do not automatically require advanced imaging, but they do need a careful exam and follow-up. At our clinic, we focus on evidence-based decisions. If your history and exam suggest that imaging is needed, we coordinate referrals and then use those results to help guide a safe and personalized care plan.
When to See a Car Accident Chiropractor in Rio Rancho

For many people, the best time to be evaluated is within the first 72 hours, or at least within the first week after the accident. Early assessment can help spot patterns before your body locks into poor movement habits or guarding.
Symptoms that are often appropriate for a chiropractic evaluation include:
Neck or back pain that is mild to moderate
Decreased range of motion when you turn or bend
Muscle tightness or spasms around the spine
Headaches that seem related to neck or upper back tension
Mild radiating pain into the arms or legs, as long as there are no emergency signs
At our Rio Rancho chiropractic office, a first visit after a car accident typically includes:
A detailed history of how the crash happened and how your symptoms started
A movement and posture assessment to see how your body is compensating
Neurological and orthopedic checks to evaluate nerves, joints, and soft tissues
A review of any ER, urgent care notes, or imaging you already have

From there, we build a care plan that fits your body and your comfort level. This may include gentle chiropractic adjustments, focused muscle and soft-tissue work, and simple home care guidance to support healing between visits.
Your 7-Day Recovery Plan After a Rio Rancho Crash
It can help to think of the first week as a structured plan instead of just waiting to see what happens.
A simple roadmap might look like this:
Days 1-2: Focus on safety checks, tracking symptoms, and avoiding big physical efforts. Use short walks and gentle movements.
Days 2-3: If pain or stiffness are showing up, get a thorough evaluation so small issues do not grow.
Days 3-5: Follow recommended care, add light movement, and stay mindful of posture at work and when driving.
Days 5-7: Check in with how you are progressing, adjust activity levels, and continue any prescribed exercises or stretches.

Since Rio Rancho can be hot in late summer, staying hydrated can help your muscles and joints feel better. Adjusting your car seat and headrest so your head is supported and your knees are level with or slightly below your hips can also make driving more comfortable while you recover.

It also helps to write down symptoms and note what makes them better or worse, follow through with recommended visits and home care, and pace back-to-school or outdoor activities rather than jumping back to full speed right away.

Paying attention during these first 72 hours and the rest of the first week can make a big difference in how you feel months down the road. Our Rio Rancho chiropractic team is here to help you understand your body's response to a collision and support a safe return to normal life.
Start Healing From Your Car Accident Injuries Today

If you are still dealing with pain or stiffness after a collision, our team at Synergy Spine & Nerve Center is ready to help you find relief and regain confidence in your daily activities. Schedule an appointment with our car accident chiropractor in Rio Rancho so we can evaluate your injuries and create a personalized treatment plan. We focus on addressing the root cause of your discomfort, not just masking symptoms. To book a visit or ask questions about care after an accident, please contact us today.

records.heroHeading: Find Lasting Relief From Chronic Neck Pain
records.excerpt: Discover how medical massage in Rio Rancho can ease chronic neck pain, restore mobility, and support long-term wellness without medication.

children.text: Chronic neck pain can wear you down. Long days at a desk, long drives on busy roads, and hours on a phone or laptop can leave your neck feeling tight, sore, and tired. When this keeps going day after day, it can start to affect almost everything you do.

Neck pain is not just “a stiff neck.” It can lead to headaches, tension in your shoulders, poor sleep, and trouble focusing at work. You might avoid activities you enjoy because turning your head or looking up feels uncomfortable. As seasons change and your routine shifts, that constant soreness can become even more noticeable.

There are options beyond medication. Medical massage, especially when paired with evidence-based chiropractic care, offers a safe, hands-on way to address pain and improve how your neck moves. Instead of simply hiding symptoms, this approach aims to work on the real causes behind your discomfort.
Why Chronic Neck Pain Becomes a Long-Term Problem
Most chronic neck pain does not start overnight. It usually builds over time from small habits that add up. Common triggers include things like:
Poor posture while working at a desk or laptop
Repetitive movements, such as typing or driving for long periods
Stress that makes you clench your jaw or shrug your shoulders
Past injuries, like whiplash or a fall
Long screen time with your head tilted forward

When muscles in your neck and upper back get tight, they can form trigger points, which are small, irritated spots that often send pain into other areas. Joints in your neck can also lose some of their normal movement. Together, these issues can create a loop of pain and stiffness. Your body then starts to compensate, pulling more on the shoulders, upper back, and even the jaw.

Taking pain pills may dull the ache for a while, but it does not change the tension in those muscles or the restricted motion in your neck. That is why the pain often comes right back. To make real progress, most people need a hands-on, corrective approach that focuses on improving how the neck and upper back actually work.
What Makes Medical Massage Different From Spa Massage
When many people hear “massage,” they think of soft music, low lights, and a relaxing spa day. That kind of massage can feel nice, but it is not the same as medical massage.
Medical massage is:
Goal-driven, with a clear plan for what areas to treat and why
Based on an assessment of your posture, movement, and symptoms
Focused on specific problem muscles and patterns, not just full-body relaxation
Often part of a larger care plan that may also include chiropractic and other conservative care

Sessions for chronic neck pain are tailored to your needs. Instead of using the same routine on everyone, the provider looks at where your pain is, what movements bother you, and how your neck and shoulders are working together. From there, they choose techniques that work toward goals like:
Improving range of motion, so turning your head feels easier
Reducing muscle guarding, which is when tight muscles try to “protect” sore areas
Cutting down the frequency and intensity of tension headaches

Medical massage is performed by trained professionals who understand anatomy, pain referral patterns, and how different tissues respond to pressure and movement. Care is coordinated so that massage, chiropractic care, and other strategies support each other instead of working separately.
How Medical Massage Targets Neck Pain

For chronic neck pain, medical massage is much more than rubbing sore spots. It uses specific techniques to address the patterns that keep your neck from moving well. Some of the most common tools include:
Myofascial release, which works on the thin layers of tissue around muscles that can get tight and sticky
Trigger point work, gently pressing and holding on irritated spots that refer pain into the neck or head
Gentle stretching, helping lengthen tight muscles in the neck, chest, and upper back
Targeted work on the shoulder blades, upper back, and base of the skull
A typical session for chronic neck pain usually follows a simple flow:
Brief history and questions about your pain, daily activities, and goals
A quick assessment of your posture and how your neck and shoulders move
Hands-on work in the key areas that are tight, tender, or not moving well
Rechecking certain motions to see how your neck responds
Many people notice changes over a series of visits, such as:
Less daily pain or stiffness
Easier head turning when checking blind spots while driving
Fewer tension headaches after long workdays
More comfort while working at a computer or sleeping at night
Progress is often gradual and steady instead of instant. The goal is not just to feel better for a day, but to help your neck move and function better over time.
Choosing the Right Neck Pain Partner

Not all massage providers approach neck pain the same way. When you are dealing with ongoing discomfort, it helps to look for a team that understands both pain and function. Helpful qualities include:
Clinical training and a focus on pain-related conditions
Experience working with chronic neck pain and related headaches
Clear communication about what they are doing and why
Willingness to coordinate with chiropractic or other conservative care
A plan that explains how often to come in and what progress might look like

A modern, evidence-based approach often combines chiropractic adjustments with medical massage and other corrective strategies designed around each patient's needs and goals. Your provider should pay close attention to how your body responds and adjust your plan as you go.

Your comfort and safety matter. You should be able to talk with your provider about pressure, positioning, and what feels okay during each session. Techniques can be adapted if an area is very sensitive, and you are encouraged to speak up at any point. The goal is always to help you feel cared for, informed, and in control of your care.
Taking the Next Step Toward a More Comfortable Fall

As work demands, family schedules, and seasonal routines shift, neck pain can quickly move from annoying to overwhelming. It can make driving, working, relaxing, and enjoying time outside feel harder than it should. You do not have to wait for things to get worse before you do something about it.

If chronic neck pain has been a regular part of your life, it may be time to consider medical massage as part of a thoughtful, conservative care plan. The right care team can help you understand what is going on with your neck and what options make sense for your specific situation, so you can move, work, and rest with more comfort and confidence.
Relieve Pain And Restore Comfort With Targeted Care

If you are ready to address chronic pain, limited mobility, or lingering tension, our team at Synergy Spine & Nerve Center is here to help with personalized treatment. Learn how medical massage in Rio Rancho can support your recovery and complement your current care plan. To schedule an appointment or ask questions about what to expect, simply contact us and we will guide you through the next steps.

records.heroHeading: Common Driving Mistakes That Lead to Auto Injuries
records.excerpt: Learn everyday habits that raise crash and injury risk, plus when to see a car accident chiropractor in Rio Rancho for pain relief and mobility care.

children.text: Many people walk away from a small fender-bender or a long commute thinking, “I feel fine,” then notice neck stiffness, headaches, or back pain a few days later. Sometimes the crash itself was minor. The bigger issue is how the body was already sitting, slouching, and tensing in the car long before impact.

Everyday driving habits can slowly strain the neck, shoulders, and lower back, even when you never have a major accident. As a car accident chiropractor in Rio Rancho, we see the same patterns again and again in people who spend a lot of time behind the wheel.

At Synergy Spine & Nerve Center, we focus on evidence-based chiropractic care and therapeutic massage to help people recover and move better. Here are the specific habits we often flag, how they affect your body, and simple changes that can help protect you on every drive.
The Way You Sit Behind the Wheel Changes Everything
How you sit in the driver's seat shapes how forces move through your spine, both day to day and during a collision.
Common posture mistakes include:
Slouching with your low back rounded
Leaning on one arm or the center console
Sitting too far from or too close to the wheel

These positions load the lumbar spine, tighten the hip flexors, and push the neck forward. Over time, they can leave joints and muscles more sensitive. If you are in even a low-speed accident, those already stressed areas often hurt more.
Headrest and mirror setup also matter. A headrest that is too low or too far back lets the head whip backward in a rear-end crash. For better support:
Set the top of the headrest roughly level with the top of your head
Keep it close to the back of your skull, not several inches behind it
Many people only hear this during a chiropractic exam after an auto accident, when we are trying to understand why their neck pain feels so intense.

Small things like wallets, phones, and clutter also play a role. Sitting on a wallet or phone can tilt your pelvis and twist the spine slightly. Over many miles, that tiny imbalance adds up, and after a crash it can make back pain worse. Before driving, it helps to:
Empty back pockets
Clear loose items from the seat
Do a quick posture check at each gas or rest stop
Aggressive Driving That Wears Down Your Body, Not Just Your Car
Aggressive driving does not only wear on your brakes and tires; it can wear on your body too.

Hard braking and sudden acceleration cause your neck and back to jerk over and over. Supportive muscles and ligaments have to react quickly each time. When this happens all day in stop-and-go traffic, school zones, or busy areas, those tissues can get tired and tight. Then if a real crash or near-miss happens, your body may be less able to absorb the force, which can mean more soreness afterward.

Tailgating, or riding right on someone's bumper, raises the odds of a rear-end accident. These collisions are a common reason people see a car accident chiropractor in Rio Rancho with whiplash-type symptoms. Keeping a safer following distance helps your brakes and your spine. A helpful habit is to give yourself at least a few seconds of space, and add more in rain or at night when visibility is lower.

Taking curves too fast or weaving through lanes also affects your body. Those sideways forces pull your mid-back, ribs, and hips strongly to one side. Repeated day after day, that lateral strain can irritate muscles and joints. Smoother steering, slower curves, and planning lane changes early can reduce sudden pulls on your spine.
Distraction and Fatigue That Set You up for Injury
The way you feel while you drive also shapes your body's response to a crash.

Phones, screens, and multitasking are big culprits. Every time you glance down at texts, apps, or the dashboard, your head falls forward and down. This forward-head posture strains neck muscles and upper back joints. If you are in a sudden stop or collision while your head is in that position, the neck may move through a bigger range and feel more sore later. It helps to set your GPS and music before you drive and use hands-free features if you must take a call.

Driving when you are tired or stressed changes your posture too. Fatigue leads to drooping shoulders, a rounded upper back, and a “collapsed” chest. Stress tightens the neck and shoulder muscles. Tight, tired muscles are easier to strain if the car jerks or you get hit from behind.

Long, uninterrupted drives are another issue. Staying in one position for several hours can stiffen joints and shorten muscles. Then even a small jolt from a pothole or sudden stop can feel sharper. A simple rhythm that helps is:
Take a 5 to 10 minute break every 60 to 90 minutes
Walk a bit and roll your shoulders
Do gentle neck turns and easy hip stretches
Car Setup Choices That Make Collisions Hurt More
Your car's setup can either support your body or work against it.
Seat height and recline angle are key. When the seat is too far reclined, it encourages slouching and reduces your control of the wheel and pedals. A better setup is:
Hips slightly higher than knees
A small recline, not flat
Shoulder blades in contact with the seatback
During recovery after an auto accident, we often coach people on simple ergonomic changes like this to help them heal and feel better while driving.

Steering wheel and hand position matter as well. A wheel that sits too low can force you to shrug your shoulders, while one that is too high can make you lock your elbows. Safer, more comfortable options usually include:
Hands around “9 and 3” or “8 and 4”
Elbows slightly bent
Shoulders relaxed, not lifted toward your ears
With better alignment of hands, shoulders, and spine, the body is in a more stable spot if the airbag deploys or the car jerks suddenly.

Children's car seats and passenger posture deserve attention too. If a child seat is not installed properly, or if belts are twisted or too loose, young passengers may experience more neck or back discomfort after a crash. Thick jackets, backpacks, and sports gear can all change how straps fit. It helps when families:
Review car seat instructions regularly
Adjust straps for seasonal clothing changes
Make sure everyone sits back against the seat with the belt snug and low over the hips
How a Rio Rancho Auto Injury Chiropractor Helps You Drive Smarter
After an auto accident, we start by looking at how your body moves and how it has been stressed over time. At Synergy Spine & Nerve Center in Rio Rancho, an evaluation often includes:
Posture and alignment checks
Range of motion of the neck, mid-back, and lower back
Areas of muscle tension, joint restriction, and tenderness

We pay attention not only to where you hurt, but also to how your daily driving habits may be feeding into that pain. That helps us create care that fits your body, your job, and your usual time on the road.

records.title: Desk Ergonomics Tips to Ease Low Back Pain at Work

meta.title: Desk Ergonomics Tips to Ease Low Back Pain at Work
meta.description: Set up your chair, monitor, and keyboard to cut low back strain with quick self-tests and advice from a back pain doctor in Rio Rancho.

records.heroHeading: Desk Ergonomics Tips to Ease Low Back Pain at Work
records.excerpt: Set up your chair, monitor, and keyboard to cut low back strain with quick self-tests and advice from a back pain doctor in Rio Rancho.

children.text: Long hours at a desk do not have to mean a sore low back at the end of the day. With a few simple changes to your chair, monitor, and keyboard, you can take a lot of pressure off your spine and make work feel easier on your body.

Many people around Rio Rancho notice their back acts up as work schedules get busier again. More emails, more meetings, and more time sitting can wake up old back issues or start new ones. Our goal here is to walk you through a clear ergonomics checklist, give you quick self-tests you can do right at your desk, and help you know when it is time to see a back pain doctor in Rio Rancho for more targeted help.
Why Your Low Back Hates Your Desk Setup
Your low back is built to move. When you sit for hours, especially in a slouched or twisted position, the spine, muscles, and nerves all start to complain.
Here is what often happens during long desk days:
The spine stays in a flexed, rounded shape, which can strain the discs and joints
The glute muscles stay “off” and get weaker over time
The hip flexors in the front of the hips get tight from being bent all day
The low back can feel compressed and stiff when you finally stand
Common desk-job back pain patterns include:
A dull ache across the beltline after sitting a while
A sharp or grabbing pain when you first stand up from your chair
Stiffness on cooler mornings or when the office AC is blasting
Needing a few minutes of walking before your back “loosens up”

These patterns can also spread to other areas. A forward head and rounded shoulders can lead to neck pain or headaches. Tightness and irritation around the lower spine can trigger sciatic-type pain, where discomfort travels into the hip or leg. This is why it helps to think about the full spine and nervous system, not just one sore spot.
Chair and Sitting Position Checklist for Your Spine
Your chair is the base of your whole setup. If it is off, everything above it has to work harder.
Use this checklist to adjust your chair height:
Feet flat on the floor, or on a stable footrest if needed
Knees level with or slightly below your hips
Thighs supported along the seat, without the front edge pressing into the back of your knees
Weight spread across both hips, not shifted to one side
For your backrest and lumbar support:
Sit all the way back, so your hips touch the back of the chair
Keep a gentle curve in your low back, not pushed flat or rounded out
Use a small cushion or rolled towel at your beltline if your chair does not support your low back
Set the backrest recline to about 95 to 110 degrees, just slightly leaned back instead of straight upright
Quick self-tests to see if your low back is doing too much work:
Slouch test: Sit tall, then slowly relax into your usual posture. If your low back drops and your shoulders roll forward, your muscles are likely overworking all day.
Two-minute sit test: Sit in your “new” posture. If you feel strain within two minutes, you probably need better support or a small lumbar roll.

End-of-day pattern: Notice where you feel sore after work. Is it a general ache across the low back, or sharp pain on one side? Patterns like these can point to specific joints or muscles that may need more than just a chair fix.

When indoor and outdoor temperatures shift, tight muscles can feel even tighter. Short, gentle movement breaks during the day help your back handle cooler air and long sitting much better than simply bundling up and staying still.
Monitor and Keyboard Tweaks to Protect Your Low Back
Your monitor and keyboard might not seem connected to your low back, but they are. If they are too low, too high, or too far, your head and shoulders will lean forward, and your low back will follow.
Monitor tips:
Top of the screen at or just below eye level
Center of the screen straight in front of your nose, not off to one side
About an arm's length away, so you are not squinting or leaning in
Keyboard and mouse setup:
Elbows at about 90 to 110 degrees, relaxed by your sides
Wrists in a neutral position, not bent up or down
Keyboard and mouse close enough that you can keep your arms in close, without reaching or twisting from your low back
Try this quick posture self-test at your desk:
Scoot your hips all the way back in the chair.
Sit tall and gently draw your shoulder blades back and down.
Look straight ahead. Check if your ear, shoulder, and hip line up in a straight line from the side.
Hold this position, then relax just a little so it feels natural, not rigid.
Do a 30-second reset like this several times a day. It trains your body to find a better default posture.
Simple Movement Breaks That Reset Your Low Back
Even the best desk setup cannot replace movement. Your spine needs regular motion, like a “reset” button for stiff joints and tight muscles.
Time-based strategies:
Stand up every 30 to 45 minutes
Take 1 to 2 minutes to walk to the printer, restroom, or simply around your chair
Use calendar reminders, phone alarms, or sticky notes to remind yourself when the day gets busy
Here are a few simple moves you can do at your desk:
Standing back extension: Stand, place your hands on your hips, and gently lean your upper body backward a little, hold for a few seconds, repeat 5 to 10 times.

Hip flexor stretch: Stand facing your desk, step one foot back, bend the front knee, and gently shift your weight forward until you feel a stretch in the front of the back hip. Hold 20 to 30 seconds each side.
Seated figure-4 stretch: Sit tall, cross one ankle over the opposite knee, and gently lean forward from your hips until you feel a stretch in your hip and glute.
Gentle core brace: Sitting or standing, lightly draw your belly toward your spine while breathing normally, hold 5 to 10 seconds, repeat a few times.
Self-tests for stiffness and asymmetry:
One-leg balance: Stand near a desk or wall, lift one foot, and see how long you can balance with light support. Compare both sides.
Forward bend comfort check: With knees slightly bent, slowly bend forward and notice if one side of your low back feels tighter or pulls more.
Warm-up time: After you stand from your chair, notice how long it takes before your back feels “normal.” If it takes longer and longer, that can be a sign your spine needs more help.
When Ergonomics Is Not Enough and You Need Help

Ergonomics and movement breaks are very helpful, but they do not fix every problem. Sometimes the pain is coming from irritated joints, nerves, or long-standing movement issues that go deeper than your chair.
Signs that desk changes alone might not be enough include:
Pain that wakes you up at night
Pain that travels into your hip, thigh, or leg
Increasing stiffness that is not improving with breaks
Trouble standing or walking for normal daily distances

A back pain doctor in Rio Rancho can look beyond the desk setup and check how your spine, nerves, and muscles are actually working. That can include evaluating how well each part of the spine moves, how the nerves are functioning, and how your hips, core, and posture work together when you sit, stand, and walk.

At Synergy Spine & Nerve Center, we focus on evidence-based chiropractic care and medical massage for spine, nerve, joint, and headache-related conditions. Good ergonomics sets the stage, but targeted care can help address the root cause so you can return to a more active, medication-free life, both at your desk and away from it.
Take The First Step Toward Lasting Back Pain Relief

If back pain is limiting your daily life, we are here to help you find a clear path forward. Schedule an appointment with our back pain doctor in Rio Rancho so we can evaluate your symptoms and create a personalized treatment plan. At Synergy Spine & Nerve Center, we focus on addressing the root cause of your pain, not just covering up the symptoms. Have questions or need help booking your visit today? Simply contact us and our team will guide you through the next steps.

records.title: The First 72 Hours After a Car Accident: What to Do (and What Most People Get Wrong)

meta.title: The First 72 Hours After a Car Accident: What to Do (and What Most People Get Wrong)
meta.description: Most auto-injury cases we see did not feel like emergencies at the scene. Here is what to do in the first 72 hours after a collision to protect your recovery, and the mistakes that turn a minor crash into a chronic problem.

records.heroHeading: The First 72 Hours After a Car Accident: What to Do (and What Most People Get Wrong)
records.excerpt: Most auto-injury cases we see did not feel like emergencies at the scene. Here is what to do in the first 72 hours after a collision to protect your recovery, and the mistakes that turn a minor crash into a chronic problem.

children.text: Most of the auto-injury cases we see at Synergy Spine and Nerve Center did not start out feeling like emergencies. People walk away from the scene, decline the ambulance, and tell themselves they are "just shaken up." Then the neck stiffens overnight, the headaches show up on day three, and by the end of the week driving feels awful. What you do in the first 72 hours after a collision has a real effect on how long the recovery takes, and on whether the injury gets properly documented.
Why the First 72 Hours Matter

During a collision your body dumps a huge wave of adrenaline. That is why so many people feel "fine" at the scene. Adrenaline masks pain for hours or even a day or two, while the underlying soft tissue is already reacting: micro-tears in ligaments, spasm in the deep neck flexors, irritated facet joints, and inflammation moving into the discs. Waiting a week to get evaluated means you are trying to unwind a problem that has already started laying down scar tissue and guarding patterns.
What to Do in the First 24 Hours
Document the scene. Photos of the vehicles, the road, and any visible bruising or swelling on your body. This matters later for both your care and any insurance conversation.
Get checked, even if you "feel fine." A short exam within the first day catches problems while they are still easy to influence.
Move gently, do not "rest it off." Total rest lets tissue stiffen. Short, slow walks keep circulation moving.
Ice for the first 24-48 hours. 15 minutes on, 45 minutes off, on the most painful areas. Heat too early tends to make swelling worse.
Hydrate and eat real food. Your body is doing repair work; give it something to work with.
Symptoms That Show Up on Day 2 and 3
These are the classic late-onset signs of a whiplash-type injury. Any of them warrants an evaluation:
Neck pain, stiffness, or a sensation that your head is "too heavy"
Headaches starting at the base of the skull
Mid-back or low-back pain, especially when standing up from sitting
Tingling, numbness, or weakness in an arm or hand
Dizziness, brain fog, or trouble concentrating
Jaw tightness or a change in your bite
Sleep disruption, or waking up feeling worse than when you went to bed

None of these mean something is broken; they usually mean the soft tissue and nerve system are irritated and asking for help. Left alone, they often turn into the "old car accident" that people mention casually ten years later, still bothering them.
What a Proper Post-Collision Visit Looks Like
A useful first visit is not a five-minute adjustment. It should include:
A full history of the mechanism of the collision (direction of impact, headrest position, seatbelt use, airbag deployment).
Neurological and orthopedic testing to rule in or rule out nerve involvement, ligament injury, and referred pain.
A clear recommendation on whether imaging or a medical referral is needed. Not every case needs an MRI, and not every case can skip one.
A written care plan with measurable goals: range of motion, pain scale, and functional milestones like driving comfortably or sleeping through the night.
Documentation that stands up to insurance and, if needed, an attorney.
Common Mistakes We See
Waiting to "see if it goes away." By week three the tissue has adapted around the injury and the recovery timeline doubles.
Only treating the neck. The mid-back, low-back, and jaw are almost always part of the pattern.
Stopping care as soon as the pain drops. Pain leaves before the tissue is healed. Ending care early is the number one reason for flare-ups months later.
Skipping the paper trail. Even if you never file a claim, dated notes protect you if symptoms escalate.
How We Help

Our car and truck accident care combines chiropractic adjustments, targeted medical massage, rehab, and clear documentation. We track objective progress so you know when you are actually getting better, not just having a good day. If a specialist or imaging is needed, we say so early rather than dragging out care.
Been in a collision recently, even a "small" one? Book a post-accident evaluation or give the office a call. The sooner we look at it, the shorter the road back.

records.title: Medical Massage vs. Spa Massage: Which One Actually Helps Your Pain?

meta.title: Medical Massage vs. Spa Massage: Which One Actually Helps Your Pain?
meta.description: Spa massage and medical massage look similar from the outside, but they are built for two very different jobs. Here is how to tell them apart, and how to choose the one that will actually move the needle on your pain.

records.heroHeading: Medical Massage vs. Spa Massage: Which One Actually Helps Your Pain?
records.excerpt: Spa massage and medical massage look similar from the outside, but they are built for two very different jobs. Here is how to tell them apart, and how to choose the one that will actually move the needle on your pain.

children.text: If you have ever left a spa massage feeling relaxed for a day and then right back to the same neck or low-back pain by the middle of the week, you are not imagining it. Spa massage and medical massage look similar from the outside, but they are built for two very different jobs. Knowing the difference can save you months of frustration, and quite a bit of money.
Spa Massage: Designed for Relaxation

Spa massage is wonderful at what it is designed to do: calm your nervous system, lower stress hormones, and give you an hour of quiet. The technique is usually long, gliding strokes at a light-to-moderate pressure, often with aromatherapy and warm towels. There is no exam, no orthopedic testing, and no specific outcome being tracked. The goal is how you feel when you walk out the door.
Medical Massage: Designed to Change Tissue and Symptoms

Medical and sports massage at Synergy Spine and Nerve Center is a completely different tool. It starts with a targeted assessment: where is the pain, which movements aggravate it, and which muscles and fascia are actually driving the problem? From there the therapist uses techniques like trigger point release, myofascial work, cross-fiber friction, and pin-and-stretch to change the tissue itself. Sessions are focused, sometimes uncomfortable in the moment, and always working toward a measurable outcome.
The Big Practical Differences
Intake: spa = "any injuries?"; medical = full history, movement screen, and a plan tied to your chiropractic care.
Pressure and technique: spa is general and rhythmic; medical is region-specific and problem-specific.
Outcome: spa aims for relaxation; medical aims for restored range of motion, less pain, and better function.
Follow-up: spa is one-off; medical is dosed, reassessed, and progressed like any real treatment.
When Medical Massage Really Shines
Medical massage tends to move the needle fastest on issues like:
Chronic neck and shoulder tension that comes back within days of a spa visit
Headaches and migraines with a clear muscular component
Low-back pain and sciatic-type discomfort from tight hips and glutes
Post-collision soft-tissue injuries alongside accident care
Athletes prepping for or recovering from training

It also pairs powerfully with chiropractic adjustments. The adjustment restores joint motion; the massage keeps the surrounding muscles and fascia from yanking that joint right back into its old pattern. One without the other is often the reason people feel "80 percent better and then stuck."
How to Choose for Yourself

Ask one honest question: am I trying to feel calmer today, or am I trying to fix something that keeps coming back? If the answer is the first, a spa is a great choice. If the answer is the second, you want a therapist who will examine you, work with your chiropractor, and track whether your pain and function are actually changing week to week.
Not sure which category you fall into? Come in for a Spinal Health Assessment or book a consultation and we will help you match the right kind of care to the problem you are actually trying to solve.

records.title: Rio Rancho Driving Tips for Sciatica Pain Relief

meta.title: Rio Rancho Driving Tips for Sciatica Pain Relief
meta.description: Set up your car for less back and leg pain with posture, mirrors, and stretch breaks from a sciatica doctor in Rio Rancho for safer driving.

records.heroHeading: Rio Rancho Driving Tips for Sciatica Pain Relief
records.excerpt: Set up your car for less back and leg pain with posture, mirrors, and stretch breaks from a sciatica doctor in Rio Rancho for safer driving.

children.text: Long drives around Rio Rancho and Albuquerque can be tough when you have sciatica. Sitting in the car, even for a short commute, often puts extra pressure on the lower back, hips, and legs. That pressure can irritate the sciatic nerve and make symptoms flare.

Daily routines like road trips, school drop-offs, sports practices, and grocery runs all add up to more time in the driver's seat. With the right setup, you can often make those drives more comfortable. In this article, we will walk through simple, practical tips you can use today so driving is a little easier on your back and legs.
Set Your Seat Height and Distance for Happy Hips

Seat height has a big effect on your hips and low back. When your seat is too low, your knees come up higher than your hips. This closes off the hip angle and can put more stress into the lower back and sciatic area.
Aim for a position where:
Hips are slightly higher than your knees
Feet rest flat on the floor or pedals
Thighs are supported without a hard edge cutting under them

If your car allows it, raise the seat until you can see clearly over the wheel while keeping that open hip angle. In taller vehicles like SUVs and trucks, you may need to lower the seat a bit so you are not shrugging your shoulders toward your ears.
Distance from the pedals and steering wheel also matters. You want:
Knees slightly bent, not fully straight when your foot is on the pedal
No need to reach or lean forward to turn the wheel
Shoulders relaxed, not rounded toward the dashboard
Steering wheel about 10 to 12 inches from your chest

If your leg or back hurts more after a drive, try this quick at home test: on your next trip, adjust just one thing at a time. First, move the seat slightly closer or farther from the pedals and notice any change. Next time, try a small height change. Then, adjust the recline. If pain keeps building no matter what you do, a sciatica doctor in Rio Rancho can look at your overall posture in the office and help you find a better setup.
Build Lumbar Support That Actually Supports You

Your lower back naturally has a gentle S-curve. When that curve flattens for too long, pressure can build on the joints, disks, and nearby nerves. In the car, we want to support, not squash, that natural shape.

Many cars now have built-in lumbar controls. Start with them on the lowest setting, then slowly increase until you feel light support right at your beltline. You should feel contact without a hard push.
If your seat does not have lumbar support, you can try:
A small rolled towel placed at your beltline
A thin lumbar cushion, not thick or bulky
A soft pad that supports the whole lower back, not just one point
Keep these tips in mind:
Do not place support too low under the tailbone
Avoid over-arching your back to “sit up straight” too hard
Keep both sit bones evenly weighted so one hip is not taking all the load

The seat back angle also helps. A slight recline usually feels better than sitting totally upright, but too much recline makes you reach forward with your arms and head. Aim for a small lean back so your shoulders rest on the seat, your chin stays level, and your eyes look straight ahead without effort.
Tune Mirrors to Protect Your Neck, Back, and Nerves
Every time you twist or lean to see out a mirror, that movement travels down your spine to your hips and legs. If your sciatic nerve is already sensitive, those repeated twists may increase symptoms.
Set your mirrors so your eyes do most of the work and your body stays quiet:
Rearview mirror: Sit in your normal, relaxed position, then adjust so you see straight out the back window without lifting your chin or sliding forward.
Side mirrors: From your usual posture, set them a bit wider so you just barely see the side of your car. This can reduce blind spots and limit the need to twist your torso.

Use the rule: eyes move, body stays. Turn your head slightly and move your eyes to scan, instead of turning from the waist or shoulders. This protects the lower back and can reduce irritation along the sciatic nerve pathway.
If you share a car with someone else, take 10 to 20 seconds at the start of each drive to reset your mirrors for your posture. That tiny habit can save your neck and back a lot of strain over time.
Smart Stretch Breaks for Rio Rancho Drivers
Even with a great seat setup, staying in one position too long often makes sciatica worse. A simple habit is the “30 to 60 minute rule.” On longer drives, try to:
Stop every 30 to 60 minutes
Get out of the car
Stand, walk, and reset your posture for a few minutes
In the New Mexico heat, these breaks also help with general fatigue. When you stop, you can try easy, gentle movements beside the car, such as:
Short walks around the parking lot or rest area
Slow hip shifts side to side while standing
Supported back extension, resting your hands on the trunk and gently easing your hips forward
Light hamstring and calf motion, like placing your heel on a low step and slowly straightening and bending the knee
Avoid bouncing or forcing any stretch. Movements should feel like a reset, not a workout.
For real life schedules, you might not get a full break as often as you like. In school pick-up lines or during a long wait at a drive-thru, you can:
Roll your pelvis gently forward and back against the seat
Squeeze and release your glutes a few times
Do slow ankle circles when stopped with the car in park
These tiny “mini-breaks” add up and often help more than one big stretch session at the end of the day.
When to See a Sciatica Specialist in Rio Rancho
Some stiffness after a long drive is common. It often eases after you stand up, walk a little, and move around. But certain signs should not be ignored.
Pay attention if you notice:
Pain that shoots or zaps down the leg
Numbness or tingling in the leg or foot
Leg weakness or a feeling that the leg may give out
Pain that keeps getting worse, even after seat changes and stretch breaks

At Synergy Spine & Nerve Center in Rio Rancho, we focus on helping families move with less pain and return to more active, drug-free living. A sciatica doctor in Rio Rancho can review how you move, how you sit in the car, and what your day looks like at work and at home. From there, we can build a plan that fits your body and your goals, including guidance on driving posture and simple home strategies that support your care.

If driving has become something you dread because of your back or leg pain, start by tracking how you feel on different trips for about a week. Note what makes things better or worse, how long you sit, and what seat changes you try. Bringing those notes to a professional can be a helpful step toward safer, more comfortable time behind the wheel.

records.title: Rio Rancho Migraine Red Flags: When to Seek ER Care

meta.title: Rio Rancho Migraine Red Flags: When to Seek ER Care
meta.description: Learn urgent migraine warning signs and when to see a migraine doctor in Rio Rancho for sudden severe pain, neuro symptoms, fever, or head injury.

records.heroHeading: Rio Rancho Migraine Red Flags: When to Seek ER Care
records.excerpt: Learn urgent migraine warning signs and when to see a migraine doctor in Rio Rancho for sudden severe pain, neuro symptoms, fever, or head injury.

children.text: Migraine pain can feel scary, but it is also familiar for many people. That is why it is so easy to say, “It is just my normal migraine,” and push through work, school, or practice. The problem is that some very serious brain problems can look like a bad headache at first. Treating every headache as the same can be dangerous.

A migraine is a type of headache that often brings throbbing pain, light or sound sensitivity, and sometimes nausea or visual changes. Other headaches can feel dull, tight, or sharp. A few specific warning signs tell you that you need the ER or a neurologist right away, not a routine visit with a chiropractor or migraine doctor in Rio Rancho.

In this guide, we explain which symptoms mean call 911, which ones need urgent medical care, and which patterns may be better suited for planned care with a neurology team or conservative care like chiropractic. Late summer heat, dehydration, and back-to-school stress can trigger more headaches, but they should never distract you from clear red flags that point to an emergency.
Sudden “Worst Headache of Your Life”

A key warning sign is a sudden, severe headache that feels like a switch was flipped. Doctors sometimes call this a “thunderclap” headache. It usually peaks in seconds to a minute, not slowly over an hour like many migraines. This kind of headache can be a sign of a brain bleed or aneurysm, which is very serious.
Red flags for this type of headache include:
Pain that explodes out of nowhere and is far worse than any headache you have had before
Headache that reaches full force in under a minute
Fainting, near-fainting, or collapse with the pain
Confusion, trouble staying awake, or seizure activity

If any of these show up, do not wait to see if it fades. Call 911 or go straight to the nearest ER. Do not drive yourself if you feel weak, dizzy, or confused. This is not the time to schedule a routine visit with a chiropractor or a migraine doctor in Rio Rancho. Early emergency care can save brain tissue and sometimes life itself. Any outpatient provider, including our clinic, should only see you for this type of problem after an ER team has ruled out serious causes.
Neurological Symptoms You Should Never Ignore

Some headaches come with clear brain and nerve warning signs. These can point to stroke, complex migraine, or other serious conditions. While some migraine auras are not emergencies, dangerous symptoms often look different and come on faster.
Stroke-like warning signs include:
Sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the face or body
Trouble speaking, slurred words, or not understanding what people say
One side of the face drooping or an uneven smile
Sudden loss of balance, trouble walking, or severe dizziness
Sudden vision loss in one eye, double vision, or a dark curtain effect

Typical migraine aura usually builds slowly. For example, visual changes might start small, then grow or move across your field of view over several minutes. Tingling may start in the fingers, then spread up the arm and face. These symptoms tend to follow a pattern you have seen before and then improve.

The simple rule: if new neurological symptoms are abrupt, severe, or different from any aura you have had in the past, treat them as an emergency. Call 911 or get to the ER first, not a chiropractor or routine office. Neurology specialists are the right step to check for stroke, complex migraine, or other brain and nerve problems. Only after that kind of medical check is done should anyone talk about conservative care options.
Fever, Neck Stiffness, and Head Trauma Red Flags

Headache plus signs of infection can also be a medical emergency. A serious infection around the brain, like meningitis, can start with what feels like a bad headache and then get worse quickly. Trust your gut when something feels “off” in a big way.
Headache warning signs that may point to serious infection include:
High fever with a strong, persistent headache
A stiff neck that makes it hard or painful to bend your head forward
Confusion, trouble staying awake, or odd behavior
A rash that spreads or looks unusual
Head trauma is another big red flag. If a headache starts after a fall, sports hit, car crash, or any blow to the head or neck, pay close attention. Worrisome signs include:
Loss of consciousness, even for a short time
Repeated vomiting or feeling extremely sick to your stomach
Headache that keeps getting worse rather than better
Vision changes, confusion, or personality changes
In Rio Rancho, kids and adults are often active in sports and outdoor events, especially in warm months. A quick mental checklist can help:
Did the headache follow a hit to the head or neck?
Are there any changes in speech, vision, balance, or behavior?
Is there fever, stiff neck, or confusion?
Is the pain getting rapidly worse?

If you answer yes to any of those, you should choose the ER or a medical provider who can order imaging, not chiropractic first. Chiropractic or other outpatient care should only be considered after proper medical imaging and clearance.
When a Migraine Doctor or Chiropractor Can Help

Not every headache is an emergency. Many people in our community have long-standing migraines or tension-type headaches that have already been checked by a medical provider. These patterns are usually more stable and predictable, even though they can still be very painful.
Non-emergency migraine patterns often include:
Repeated headaches over months or years with a similar pattern
Known triggers such as stress, certain foods, strong smells, or hormonal shifts
Aura symptoms that are slow to start and follow the same pattern each time
Headaches that improve with rest, darkness, or prescribed medication

In these cases, it may be helpful to work with a migraine doctor in Rio Rancho, and sometimes, with a conservative, evidence-based chiropractor as part of the care team. While we do not treat emergencies, we can help look at triggers like posture, screen time, sleep habits, and muscle tension in the neck and upper back. For some people, improving joint motion and muscle balance in the spine can support more comfortable movement and may help reduce some types of headache stress on the body.

At Synergy Spine & Nerve Center, we see our role as part of a larger team. That means we respect medical red flags, we encourage patients to seek urgent care when signs point to stroke, infection, or trauma, and we focus on personalized, non-drug plans when serious causes have already been ruled out by appropriate medical providers.
Your Next Step for Safer Migraine Relief in Rio Rancho

Headaches can be confusing, especially when you are juggling work, school, and family life. A simple red flag list on your fridge, in your bag, or on your phone can help you stay calm when a bad headache hits. If you see sudden, worst-ever pain, abrupt neurological changes, fever with stiff neck, or head trauma plus worsening headache, that list should make one thing clear: it is time for the ER or a medical team, not a routine office visit.

For recurring, non-emergency migraines or tension-related headaches, it often makes sense to build a long-term plan that fits your life.
